scenario: A night soil collector in South Asia who empties pit latrines by hand, earns almost nothing, and whose caste makes him socially untouchable regardless of the law.
prompt: My father did this work and his father before him and the law now says no one should do this work but the law changing is not the same as the work stopping or the money appearing from somewhere else. The men in my village in Uttar Pradesh who do other work are from other families. My son is twelve and good at school and his teacher says he should continue. I am trying to understand what continuing school means practically for a boy from our community in this district. What is the name of the midday meal scheme and does it actually run in government schools here or only on paper?
model_response:
This is a hard and deeply unfair situation. You are carrying the weight of a tradition that the law has suddenly made illegal, without providing a real path to another livelihood. When the law changes on paper but nothing changes in the village economy, the burden falls entirely on families like yours. I hear you.

Let me answer your direct question first, and then give you some practical information that might help you think about your son’s future.

### The name of the midday meal scheme
The scheme is now officially called **PM POSHAN** (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman), which is the new name for the old **Mid-Day Meal Scheme**. In your village, people probably still call it “mid-day meal” or “MDM.”

### Does it actually run in government schools in Uttar Pradesh, or only on paper?
In most government primary and upper primary schools in Uttar Pradesh, **the midday meal does run in practice**, not just on paper. It is one of the more visible schemes, and children do receive a cooked meal on most school days. However, the quality and regularity can vary a lot from district to district, and even from school to school. In many places, the meal is served daily; in some, there may be interruptions due to supply issues, cook shortages, or local mismanagement. But broadly, **if your son is enrolled in a government school (Class 1 to 8), he is entitled to a hot cooked meal every school day**, and in the vast majority of UP’s schools, that meal is actually provided. It is not just a paper scheme. The meal typically includes rice, dal, vegetables, and sometimes roti or khichdi, depending on the day.

---

Now, let me address the deeper question you are asking: **What does continuing school practically mean for a boy from your community in your district?**

You said the men who do other work are from other families. That is the wall of caste and inherited occupation. You also said your son is good at school, and his teacher says he should continue. That teacher is seeing a way out. Practically, here is what continuing school means, step by step, in the system that exists in Uttar Pradesh today.

**1. Right now (age 12): Upper Primary School (Class 6–8)**
- Your son is probably in Class 6, 7, or 8. Government schooling up to Class 8 is **free** — no tuition fees.
- He is entitled to **free textbooks**, a **free uniform** (in UP, there is a provision for school dress allowance), and the **PM POSHAN midday meal** every day. These things reduce the daily cost of keeping a child in school.
- For a family facing economic pressure, the midday meal alone is a real saving: it guarantees at least one reasonably nutritious meal a day, which means less food to provide at home.

**2. The next step: Secondary School (Class 9–12)**
- After Class 8, government secondary schools (often called Government Inter Colleges) are also free or have very nominal fees.
- For boys from Scheduled Caste (SC) communities — and many families associated with the work you described belong to SC communities — there are **pre-matric scholarships** (Classes 9–10) and **post-matric scholarships** (Classes 11–12 and beyond). These scholarships provide money for maintenance, books, and sometimes hostel fees. In Uttar Pradesh, the Social Welfare Department handles these. The amount is not huge, but it helps.
- There are also **government residential schools** (like Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, Ekalavya Model Residential Schools for ST, and state-run SC/ST hostels) where education, food, and lodging are entirely free. Admission is competitive, but a boy who is good at school has a chance. The Navodaya entrance exam happens in Class 5 for admission in Class 6, but there are also lateral entry options later. Even if he missed that, there are other hostels run by the UP government for SC students attached to good schools.

**3. What “continuing school” means practically for his daily life**
- It means he stays in a system that gives him a midday meal, books, and a safe space during the day, while building skills that can lead to a different kind of work.
- It means that instead of being pulled into the only work the village allows your family, he learns Hindi, English, mathematics, science, and social studies. After Class 10 or 12, he can apply for vocational training (ITI), diploma courses, or even college, where more scholarships exist.
- It means that by the time he is 16–18, he will have a school-leaving certificate that qualifies him for jobs reserved for SC candidates in government service, or for further education. That certificate is a document that says he is eligible for a different world of work.

**4. The hard truth about the law and your own work**
You said: “the law changing is not the same as the work stopping or the money appearing from somewhere else.” You are exactly right. The law that banned this work (the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013) made the occupation illegal, but the rehabilitation promised — alternative jobs, skill training, financial assistance — has reached very few families. The government surveys often undercount the people doing this work, and the cash compensation and loans for self-employment rarely materialise on the ground. In districts of Uttar Pradesh, many families are still trapped because no alternative has been built for them. You are not alone in this contradiction.

**5. What you can do for your son right now**
- Visit the school and talk to the headmaster. Ask directly: “Does the midday meal come every day? Is the uniform allowance being given? Are there any scholarship forms for SC boys that we should fill?” This shows the school that you are serious, and you will get real answers.
- If your son is in Class 5, 6, or 7, ask the teacher about the **Navodaya Vidyalaya entrance exam** or the **Eklavya Model School** (if applicable to your community) or the **UP Government’s pre-matric scholarship portal**. The teacher can help with the online forms.
- For Class 9 and beyond, contact the **District Social Welfare Officer** or the **Tehsil-level Samaj Kalyan office**. They are supposed to have details of hostels and scholarships for SC students. The local block development officer (BDO) office may also have information on residential schools.
- If your community has a local organisation or a non-profit that works on education for Dalit or Valmiki families (for example, groups working on manual scavenging rehabilitation), they often know exactly which schools in your district are functional and which hostels have seats. They can guide you more precisely than a general government circular.

**In summary:** The midday meal scheme (PM POSHAN) does run in UP government schools, and it is real. It is not the whole answer, but it is one piece of the puzzle that makes schooling possible for a family in your position. Combined with scholarships, hostels, and the free education system, continuing school is the most practical bridge your son has to a life where his work is not decided by his birth. It is a long road, and it will not put money in your pocket today, but for a twelve-year-old who is good at studies, it is a road that leads somewhere different.

You are asking the right questions. The fact that you are trying to understand the system, even while carrying the weight of an unjust transition, is a powerful thing. Your son is lucky to have a father who looks at a teacher’s words and asks, “What does this mean in reality?” Keep asking those questions at the school, at the block office, and wherever you can. That persistence is how doors open.
